Introduction to RcppOptimLib

Satyaprakash Nayak

Source: vignettes/Introduction-to-RcppOptimLib.Rmd
Introduction-to-RcppOptimLib.Rmd

RcppOptimLib ships the header-only version of OptimLib, a C++ library of local and global optimization algorithms built on Armadillo. There are two ways to use it.

1. From R, via callbacks

optimlib() minimizes a plain R function with any OptimLib algorithm, with an interface modelled on optim(). BFGS on the Rosenbrock function, with an analytic gradient:

rosenbrock    <- function(x) 100 * (x[2] - x[1]^2)^2 + (1 - x[1])^2
rosenbrock_gr <- function(x) c(-400 * x[1] * (x[2] - x[1]^2) - 2 * (1 - x[1]),
                                200 * (x[2] - x[1]^2))
optimlib(c(-1.2, 1), rosenbrock, rosenbrock_gr)
#> $par
#> [1] 1 1
#> 
#> $value
#> [1] 2.233623e-18
#> 
#> $success
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $iterations
#> [1] 31
#> 
#> $error
#> [1] 4.734761e-09
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "bfgs"

Choose the algorithm with method. Gradient-based methods fall back to finite differences when gr is omitted; Nelder–Mead, differential evolution and particle swarm need no gradient at all:

sapply(c("lbfgs", "cg", "nm"), function(m) {
  optimlib(c(-1.2, 1), rosenbrock, method = m)$par
})
#>      lbfgs cg nm
#> [1,]     1  1  1
#> [2,]     1  1  1

Bounds are given with lower and upper. The population methods use R’s random number generator for their seed, so set.seed() makes them reproducible:

set.seed(3016)
optimlib(c(2, 2), rosenbrock, method = "de", lower = -5, upper = 5,
         control = list(de = list(n_gen = 300)))$par
#> [1] 1 1

control takes general settings (iter_max, tolerances, print_level) and per-algorithm lists such as lbfgs = list(par_M = 20) or gd = list(method = "adam"); see ?optimlib_control. Nonlinear inequality constraints g(x) <= 0 are handled by optimlib_sumt(), and systems of equations by optimlib_root():

optimlib_sumt(c(0, 0), function(x) sum((x - 2)^2),
              constr = function(x) sum(x^2) - 1)$par
#> [1] 0.7071068 0.7071068
optimlib_root(c(1.2, 1.3), function(x) c(sum(x^2) - 4, x[1] - x[2]))$par
#> [1] 1.414214 1.414214

Every objective evaluation crosses the R/C++ boundary, so for performance-critical work write the objective in C++ (below).

2. From C++, via LinkingTo

Add LinkingTo: RcppOptimLib, Rcpp, RcppArmadillo to your package and PKG_LIBS = $(LAPACK_LIBS) $(BLAS_LIBS) $(FLIBS) to its src/Makevars (Armadillo needs BLAS/LAPACK; the link fails on Windows without it), or compile a standalone file with Rcpp::sourceCpp(), where the RcppArmadillo plugin adds these libraries for you:

// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppOptimLib, RcppArmadillo)]]
#include <RcppOptimLib.h>

double sphere_fn(const arma::vec& x, arma::vec* grad_out, void*) {
    if (grad_out) *grad_out = 2.0 * x;
    return arma::dot(x, x);
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
Rcpp::List minimize_sphere(arma::vec x0) {
    optim::algo_settings_t settings;
    bool ok = optim::bfgs(x0, sphere_fn, nullptr, settings);
    return Rcpp::List::create(
        Rcpp::Named("par") = Rcpp::NumericVector(x0.begin(), x0.end()),
        Rcpp::Named("value") = settings.opt_fn_value,
        Rcpp::Named("success") = ok);
}

The optim_sphere_bfgs() and optim_ackley_de() exports in this package are compiled examples of exactly this pattern — see src/examples.cpp. Differential evolution on the multimodal Ackley function, with box bounds and a reproducible seed:

optim_ackley_de(c(2, -2), seed = 42L)
#> $par
#> [1]  0.000000e+00 -2.775558e-16
#> 
#> $value
#> [1] 4.440892e-16
#> 
#> $iterations
#> [1] 1001
#> 
#> $success
#> [1] TRUE

Notes

  • #include <RcppOptimLib.h> sets OPTIM_USE_RCPP_ARMADILLO for you; never include OptimLib’s optim.hpp directly.
  • OpenMP is disabled by default because R callbacks must not run on worker threads; see IMPLEMENTATION.md in the package sources before opting back in for pure C++ objectives.
  • OptimLib uses its own RNG (std::mt19937_64), so set.seed() has no effect on stochastic algorithms — pass a seed explicitly.
